idiom_name: OpenSSL::Cipher (AES-256-GCM) sealing a JSON/Marshal payload + inspect/marshal_dump hooks
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library ships OpenSSL bindings, so the encryption strategy is OpenSSL::Cipher.new('aes-256-gcm') with encrypt, a random iv and an auth_tag sealing the protected payload, and the transfer object is an ordinary class whose inspect/to_s are overridden so p, interpolation and logger output never render the protected hash, while marshal_dump/marshal_load decide what Marshal writes. What replaces the classic structure: the cipher plus the marshal hook pair replaces the class's encrypted data map, and Object#inspect is the masking hook for the masked-list variant. Sealing a JSON payload is preferable to Marshal for anything that will be loaded back, because Marshal.load reconstructs arbitrary objects.
code_sketch:
class ObfuscatedTO
  def seal(key)
    c = OpenSSL::Cipher.new("aes-256-gcm").encrypt
    c.key = key
    @sealed = c.random_iv + c.update(JSON.generate(@protected)) + c.final + c.auth_tag
    @protected.clear                              # drop the plaintext copy
  end
  def unseal(key)                                 # iv||ct||tag; tag failure -> CipherError
    iv, tag, data = @sealed.unpack("a12a16a*")
    c = OpenSSL::Cipher.new("aes-256-gcm").decrypt
    c.key, c.iv, c.auth_tag = key, iv, tag
    JSON.parse(c.update(data) + c.final)
  end
  def inspect = "#<ObfuscatedTO id=#{@id}>"        # never @protected or @sealed
end
pitfalls: Marshal.load reconstructs arbitrary objects and the docs call it unsuitable for untrusted data: verify the AEAD tag before loading and prefer JSON for the payload, or the sealed envelope becomes a remote-code-execution vector instead of a protection.

Overriding inspect/to_s covers p, puts and interpolation, but not marshal_dump (which writes every instance variable unless overridden), ActiveSupport as_json, pretty-printers, or debugger variable views - define marshal_dump/_dump and the JSON view deliberately.
OpenSSL::Cipher is one-shot: a wrong key, wrong iv or tampered tag raises OpenSSL::Cipher::CipherError, which must be handled as tampering (fail closed) rather than retried or rescued broadly.

Ruby strings are mutable so String#clear can wipe a buffer, but interning, frozen-string deduplication and GC copies make erasure best-effort; avoid converting secrets to symbols, which are not collectable.
